what-makes-a-model-multimodal.explain:
## What it is

A **multimodal model** accepts, produces, or both, more than one kind of data (modality): text, images, audio, video. In practice most "multimodal LLMs" take images or audio *in* and produce text *out*.

**How it works.** Every modality is converted into a sequence of vectors the transformer can attend over. Text goes through a tokenizer and embedding table. An image goes through a vision encoder that turns patches into embeddings, then a projector maps them into the same dimension as text embeddings. After that the transformer sees one mixed sequence, for example `[text tokens][image tokens][text tokens]`.

**Why it matters.** One model can reason over a screenshot and the question about it together, instead of you wiring several systems.

**How it goes wrong.** "Multimodal" is not one capability. A model may read images well but not generate them, or accept audio but only through an internal transcriber. Always ask: which modalities in, which out, and how reliable per modality.

A multimodal model turns images, audio, or video into tokens and runs them through the same transformer that already handles text. Native models were trained on mixed data. A bolted-on pipeline runs ASR, OCR, or a captioner first, then a text-only LLM. Text is still the interlingua: reasoning and almost always the output happen in text-like tokens. “Any-to-any” usually means several inputs and text out.

The checklist line to keep in your head is: What makes a model multimodal. Understand what makes a model multimodal: images, audio, and video are converted into tokens and fed into the same transformer that already processes text.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, what makes a model multimodal is how you avoid a class of incidents this module exists to catch. You pick native versus pipeline on latency, cost, and how errors compound — not on a launch video.

The concrete requirement is: Understand what makes a model multimodal: images, audio, and video are converted into tokens and fed into the same transformer that already processes text. If you cannot show an artefact for that sentence, you are still in demo mode.

In interviews, multimodal vs a pipeline: one model versus ASR-then-LLM; say what each throws away (tone, layout) and what still carries over from text LLMs (window, sampling, failures). A strong answer names this item (What makes a model multimodal) and the next action, not a vendor logo.

## How it works + one small example

Treat “What makes a model multimodal” as a control you can point at, not a slogan. Understand what makes a model multimodal: images, audio, and video are converted into tokens and fed into the same transformer that already processes text.

List input modalities, whether you need native joint attention, and what you are willing to lose. If you only need a transcript, a pipeline may win. If you need layout or prosody, native or a specialist plus checks.

A meeting assistant that only searches text can transcribe then RAG. A meeting assistant that must notice sarcasm needs audio tokens or at least prosody features, not a flattened transcript alone.

Write the control in the release notes for m12-1: what you changed, which gold set you scored, and how you would undo it. If you cannot undo it, you do not yet operate it.

## Failure modes

1. **Skipping “What makes a model multimodal” because the happy path works.** Understand what makes a model multimodal: images, audio, and video are converted into tokens and fed into the same transformer that already processes text. Calling a captioner+LLM “multimodal” and being surprised layout died.

2. **Doing it once and never again.** A control that is not in CI, a runbook, or a dashboard dies after the demo. Believing any-to-any means you can emit video today.

3. **Confusing a tool with the control.** Buying a vendor does not implement what makes a model multimodal. Forgetting image tokens share the text context window.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

What makes a model multimodal: Understand what makes a model multimodal: images, audio, and video are converted into tokens and fed into the same transformer that already processes text. Native joint tokens versus a pipeline; text is the interlingua; pick on compounding error, cost, and what the pipeline discards. I can show the artefact, the metric, and the undo. If I cannot, I will not call the system production-ready.

## A concrete walk-through

You are on the hook for m12-1. A reviewer asks you to prove “What makes a model multimodal.” You draw one transformer with two encoders, then a stacked ASR→LLM. You mark where tone and layout die. You keep the text window math on both pictures.

You do not tell a story about intentions. You open the artefact that implements Understand what makes a model multimodal: images, audio, and video are converted into tokens and fed into the same transformer that already processes text. You change one lever, re-run the same eval command, and show the before/after. Then you undo the lever and show the metric return. That loop is the walk-through.

questions.a: The image is split into patches, a vision encoder turns them into embeddings, and a projector maps these into the text embedding space so they sit in the same token sequence the transformer attends over alongside text tokens.

questions.a: Which modalities go in and which come out (image in does not imply image out). Whether the processing is native or a hidden pipeline (e.g. a separate transcriber). How reliable it is on your specific data type, tested on your own samples rather than a demo.

native-multimodal-vs-bolted-on-pipeline.explain:
## What it is

Two ways to build a system that handles images or audio.

**Bolted-on pipeline:** specialist models convert everything to text first (OCR, speech-to-text, an image captioner), then a text-only LLM reasons over that text. Each stage is separate, swappable and cheap to debug.

**Native multimodal:** one model is trained on text and other modalities together, so non-text content reaches the same transformer as embeddings. It can attend directly to pixels or sound features while answering.

**Trade-offs.**
- Pipelines: modular, cheaper per stage, easy to inspect intermediate text, but lossy at every hand-off and errors compound (a bad transcript becomes a confident wrong answer).
- Native: keeps tone, layout, spatial relations, and handles questions the converter never anticipated; but it is a black box, costs more tokens, and you cannot inspect what it 'saw'.

**Interview angle:** the right answer is rarely ideological. Choose by what information must survive and how much auditability you need. Many production systems mix both: OCR for exact text plus a vision model for layout.

text-as-the-interlingua.explain:
## What it is

In a pipeline design, **text is the interlingua**: the common language every component speaks. Speech becomes a transcript, an image becomes a caption or OCR text, and the LLM only ever sees strings.

**Why teams do this.** Text is cheap, inspectable, loggable, searchable and works with every existing tool (RAG, evals, guardrails, diffing). You can unit-test the transcript independently of the reasoning.

**The catch.** Anything text cannot express is discarded at the boundary: speaker emotion, emphasis, background sound, handwriting style, chart geometry, which cell a number sat in. The LLM then reasons confidently over an incomplete record, and nothing flags what was dropped.

**Practical rule.** Use text as the interlingua when the task truly is about the words. When the task depends on how something looked or sounded, keep the original modality in the loop, or store both the text and a pointer to the source so a human or a vision model can recheck.

what-carries-over-from-text-llms.explain:
## What it is

Most of what you know about text LLMs still applies once an image or audio clip is in the context.

**Carries over:**
- **Context window and cost**: non-text inputs are tokens too and count against the limit and the bill.
- **Prompting**: clear instructions, examples, output schemas, and structured output work the same way.
- **Sampling and hallucination**: the model still generates plausibly rather than verifying, so it can describe things that are not there.
- **Evaluation discipline**: you still need a labelled test set, regression runs and error analysis.
- **Prompt injection**: text inside an image (a sign, a screenshot, a PDF page) can carry instructions; treat it as untrusted data.
- **RAG, caching, routing, guardrails**: the same architectural patterns apply.

**What is new:** token counts depend on resolution or duration, perception errors (counting, small text) replace some reasoning errors, and the data may be sensitive in new ways (faces, voices).

An interviewer often checks whether you reflexively reapply sound LLM engineering rather than treating multimodal as magic.

A multimodal model turns images, audio, or video into tokens and runs them through the same transformer that already handles text. Native models were trained on mixed data. A bolted-on pipeline runs ASR, OCR, or a captioner first, then a text-only LLM. **Any-to-any** describes a model or product that can take any supported modality in and produce any supported modality out: text to image, audio to text, image to speech, and so on, ideally in one conversation.

**What it usually means in reality.**
- A single model family or API surface exposes several input and output types, but each pairing may be supported to a different quality level.
- Output generation may be handled by separate decoders (an image decoder, an audio decoder) behind a shared reasoning core, or by a router that calls different specialist models.
- Marketing claims rarely say which pairs are strong and which merely work.

**How to evaluate it.** Build a matrix of the input-output pairs you need, test each on your own data, and record quality, latency and cost per cell. A strong text-to-text cell says nothing about audio-to-audio.

**Failure mode:** assuming coverage is uniform, then discovering the one pair your product depends on (say, image in, accurate structured JSON out) is the weakest.

what-a-pipeline-throws-away.explain:
## What it is

When a pipeline converts a modality into text, the conversion is a **lossy compression**. It keeps what the converter was built to capture and drops the rest.

**Typical losses**
- *Speech to text*: tone, emotion, emphasis, pauses, who spoke when (unless diarization is added), background sounds, accents flattened by normalization.
- *Image to caption/OCR*: spatial relations, colour, exact positions, chart shapes, diagram structure, anything not described.
- *PDF to text*: reading order, table cell alignment, footnote links, figures.

**Why it is dangerous:** the loss is invisible downstream. The LLM never knows a table was flattened, so it answers fluently from garbled rows.

**What to do**
1. Decide up front which signals the task needs; if they are non-textual, keep the original modality.
2. Preserve structure where possible (Markdown tables, bounding boxes, timestamps, speaker labels).
3. Keep a pointer to the source so low-confidence cases can be rechecked.
4. Evaluate end to end, not just the converter's own accuracy.

A multimodal model turns images, audio, or video into tokens and runs them through the same transformer that already handles text. Native models were trained on mixed data. A bolted-on pipeline runs ASR, OCR, or a captioner first, then a text-only LLM. Text is still the interlingua: reasoning and almost always the output happen in text-like tokens. “Any-to-any” usually means several inputs and text out.

patches-the-vision-encoder.explain:
## What it is

A vision-language model does not see pixels as a picture; it sees a sequence of **patch embeddings**.

**Mechanism.** The image is resized and cut into a grid of fixed-size square patches (for example 14x14 or 16x16 pixels). Each patch is flattened and linearly projected into a vector, position information is added, and a **vision encoder** (typically a Vision Transformer) lets patches attend to each other. A small **projector** (linear layer, MLP, or a resampler/query module) then maps the encoder's outputs into the language model's embedding space. Those vectors are the "image tokens".

**Illustrative numbers.** A 336x336 image with 14-pixel patches gives 24x24 = 576 patches, so roughly 576 image tokens before any compression.

**Why it matters.** The patch size sets the finest detail the model can resolve: text smaller than a patch becomes mush. The encoder is usually pretrained with a contrastive objective (CLIP-style) or similar, which biases it toward semantics over exact pixel detail.

**Failure mode:** assuming the model measures pixels precisely. It reasons over summarized patch features.

A vision encoder tiles an image into patches and embeds each patch. Token count scales with resolution and tiling, not with JPEG size. High-detail modes send many tiles. Downscaling kills small text, thin lines, and chart labels. Those tokens share the text window.

The checklist line to keep in your head is: Patches & the vision encoder. Understand how a vision encoder splits an image into a grid of patches and turns each patch into a vector the transformer can consume.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, patches & the vision encoder is how you avoid a class of incidents this module exists to catch. A screenshot that looks fine to you can be texture to the model. Resolution and crop policy are product decisions.

The concrete requirement is: Understand how a vision encoder splits an image into a grid of patches and turns each patch into a vector the transformer can consume. If you cannot show an artefact for that sentence, you are still in demo mode.

Treat “Patches & the vision encoder” as a control you can point at, not a slogan. Understand how a vision encoder splits an image into a grid of patches and turns each patch into a vector the transformer can consume.

Choose resolution vs tile count. Prefer a crop of the table over a 4k desktop. Count image tokens against the window before you add history.

## What it is

High-resolution images do not fit a single encoder pass at full detail, so many systems use **tiling**: split the image into several tiles, encode each, and often add a downscaled overview of the whole image.

**How it works.** The image is resized so its sides fit a tile grid (for example 2x3 tiles of fixed size), and every tile yields its own block of tokens. Some APIs expose a **detail** setting (such as low, high or auto): low sends a small downscaled view for a flat, cheap token cost; high enables tiling for fine detail at higher cost. Exact names and formulas vary by provider, so check current docs.

**When to choose what**
- Low detail: classifying scenes, identifying the main object, colour, rough layout.
- High detail: reading small text, dense charts, receipts, UI screenshots.

**How it goes wrong.** Using low detail for document reading yields unreadable text and hallucinated numbers; using high detail for thumbnails wastes money. Tile boundaries can also slice a word or object in half.

**Rule:** pick detail by the smallest feature you must read, then verify on a sample.

## What it is

Image tokens live in the **same context window** as text. There is no separate image budget.

**Implications**
- The window limit applies to the sum of system prompt, history, images and the output reservation.
- In a multi-turn chat, images from earlier turns are re-sent each turn unless you drop or replace them, so cost and latency compound over a conversation.
- Many images in one request crowd out room for retrieved text or long instructions.

4. Cap images per request and tell users the limit.

**Failure mode:** a chat that works for three images fails or slows badly at thirty.

what-vision-models-do-well.explain:
## What it is

Modern vision-language models are strong at **semantic, holistic understanding** of images.

**Reliable strengths**
- Describing scenes and identifying common objects, activities and settings.
- Reading clear, reasonably large printed text in natural images and screenshots.
- Answering questions that combine perception and world knowledge ("what is unusual about this kitchen?").
- Understanding UI screenshots, simple charts, diagrams and memes at a gist level.
- Classification and tagging with natural-language labels, with no retraining.
- Extracting structured fields from clean, well-lit documents.

**Why**: the encoder is trained on huge image-text data to capture meaning, and the language model supplies reasoning and knowledge.

**Using it well.** Ask for the gist, comparisons, and descriptions; give a schema for extraction; supply a few labelled examples for domain terms.

**Boundaries.** Strength at semantics does not imply precision: the same model that explains a meme may miscount ten items or misread a small digit. Treat "does well" as a statement about typical, clear inputs, and verify on your own data before relying on it.

Vision models read text in images, describe scenes, pull named fields, and sketch charts. They fail at precise counting, geometry, dense tables, and they invent labels that were never there. They generate a plausible description of patches; they do not measure. Ask “how reliably on my invoices?” not “can it read invoices?”

## What it is

Three well-known weak spots: **counting, spatial reasoning, and dense tables**.

**Counting.** Models estimate rather than enumerate. Small counts (1-5) are usually fine; larger counts, overlapping or similar objects, and crowded scenes drift. Answers are often plausible round numbers.

**Spatial relations.** "Is the red cup left of the laptop?", relative sizes, which line connects to which node, and distances can be wrong because patch features encode appearance more than precise geometry. Left/right from the viewer's versus the subject's perspective is a classic trap.

**Dense tables.** Many rows and columns, merged cells, thin gridlines and small fonts cause skipped rows, shifted columns, and values attached to the wrong header.

- Count with a detector or ask the model to list items individually, then count the list.

- Prefer structured output with per-row entries.

## What it is

A vision model can **describe things that are not in the image**, or state text and numbers that it did not truly read. This is hallucination with a visual flavor.

**Common forms**
- Invented objects or attributes ("a man holding an umbrella" when nothing is held).
- Completed text: a partially legible sign or serial number is finished with plausible characters.
- Plausible-but-wrong numbers in charts and tables.
- Confident answers about content outside the crop or beyond the resolution.
- Following the question's presupposition ("what colour is the cat?" when there is no cat).

**Why it happens.** The language model prior fills gaps; the encoder gives a lossy summary; training rewards fluent answers rather than "I can't tell".

**Reducing it**
1. Allow and encourage "unreadable" or "not visible" as valid outputs, with an explicit schema field.
2. Ask for quoted evidence or locations.
3. Avoid leading questions.
4. Crop and enlarge uncertain regions, then re-ask.
5. Cross-check with OCR or a second pass.

**Risk framing:** the most dangerous fabrications are plausible ones in high-stakes fields such as medical, legal, or financial images.

To fix vision errors you need a mental model of where they come from. Roughly four layers.

1. **Input loss**: blur, glare, low resolution, compression, downscaling before the encoder. Information gone before the model starts.
2. **Encoder limits**: patch size, semantic-focused pretraining, and lossy compression into a fixed number of tokens mean exact geometry, small glyphs and fine counts are weakly represented.
3. **Alignment gaps**: the projector must translate visual features into the LLM's language space; rare concepts (specialist diagrams, medical imagery, unusual scripts) may be poorly aligned.
4. **Language prior**: the LLM completes patterns and prefers plausible answers over "I can't see that".

**Diagnostic habit.** Ask: could a human read the answer from exactly what was sent? If no, it is input loss. If yes but the model fails, change the representation (crop, tile, OCR) or accept a perception limit. If the content is specialist, consider examples or fine-tuning.

**Common trap:** trying to fix a perception failure with a longer prompt. Prompts help with reasoning and format, not with pixels that were never encoded.

## What it is

A PDF is a container, not a content type. Two very different things hide inside the extension.

**Text-layer (born-digital) PDFs** store characters with positions and fonts. You can extract exact text, often with coordinates, quickly and almost free, with no recognition errors.

**Scans** are images of pages (sometimes with an invisible OCR layer added). There are no real characters until OCR or a vision model reads them, so quality depends on resolution, skew, lighting and noise.

**How to tell.** Try extracting text: near-empty output or odd garbage means scan; also check for embedded fonts and image-only pages. Mixed documents exist (scanned pages stapled into digital ones), so decide per page.

**Why it matters.** Digital text extraction is more accurate and far cheaper than vision for the characters themselves, but it can lose layout and reading order. Scans need OCR or vision, which cost more and introduce errors.

**Routing rule:** use the text layer when present and sane, fall back to OCR/vision for scans, and add vision when layout or figures matter. A scanned file with a poor invisible OCR layer is a common trap: text 'exists' but is wrong.

Documents split into text-layer PDFs versus scans. OCR and native vision trade accuracy, cost, layout. Reading order, tables, and charts each fail differently. Extract into a schema, ground fields to a page region, route low confidence. Visual RAG is pages as retrieval units — expensive, sometimes necessary. Clean digital text rarely needs page images. Dedicated OCR still wins on forms.

The checklist line to keep in your head is: Text-layer PDFs vs scans. Distinguish a digital PDF that carries its own text layer from a scan or photograph where every character has to be recovered from pixels.

ocr-vs-native-vision-reading.explain:
## What it is

Two ways to get characters out of an image.

**OCR (optical character recognition).** A specialized model detects text regions and recognizes characters, returning text with boxes and confidence scores. Deterministic-ish, fast, cheap, good at exact characters in clear print, and it never 'hallucinates' beyond what it recognizes (it makes character errors instead). It is weak at understanding layout semantics.

**Native vision reading.** A multimodal LLM reads the image holistically. It understands layout, labels, tables and context, and can answer questions directly, but can paraphrase, skip, or fabricate text, costs more, and gives no per-character confidence.

**Choosing**
- Exact IDs, amounts, serial numbers: OCR or text layer, validated.
- Semantic extraction from varied layouts: vision LLM.
- Best practice for hard documents: **both**: OCR text and the page image into the LLM, which uses OCR for characters and vision for structure.

**Interview probe:** "Why not just use the LLM for everything?" Cost, speed, auditability, and fabricated-text risk.

Documents split into text-layer PDFs versus scans. OCR and native vision trade accuracy, cost, layout. Reading order, tables, and charts each fail differently. Extract into a schema, ground fields to a page region, route low confidence. Visual RAG is pages as retrieval units — expensive, sometimes necessary. Clean digital text rarely needs page images. Dedicated OCR still wins on forms.

The checklist line to keep in your head is: OCR vs native vision reading. Compare OCR-based reading with native vision reading by a multimodal model on accuracy, cost, latency, and how much layout they preserve.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, oCR vs native vision reading is how you avoid a class of incidents this module exists to catch. Enterprise PDFs are where multimodal systems earn or lose trust.

The concrete requirement is: Compare OCR-based reading with native vision reading by a multimodal model on accuracy, cost, latency, and how much layout they preserve. If you cannot show an artefact for that sentence, you are still in demo mode.

In interviews, schema before prompt, cite the page, know when plain text beats pixels, know when a specialist OCR is cheaper than a frontier vision call. A strong answer names this item (OCR vs native vision reading) and the next action, not a vendor logo.

## How it works + one small example

Treat “OCR vs native vision reading” as a control you can point at, not a slogan. Compare OCR-based reading with native vision reading by a multimodal model on accuracy, cost, latency, and how much layout they preserve.

Detect text layer. If present, extract text+layout. If scan, decide OCR vs native vision vs both. Define fields first. Validate. Ground. Hybrid retrieve. Price tokens.

## What it is

Documents are two-dimensional; language models consume one-dimensional sequences. **Reading order** is how you serialize the page.

**Hazards**
- Multi-column text read straight across rows, interleaving columns.
- Headers, footers, page numbers and watermarks injected mid-paragraph.
- Sidebars, captions and footnotes placed in the wrong spot.
- Tables flattened into lines with no cell structure.
- Rotated or mixed-orientation regions.

**How to handle**
1. Use layout analysis to detect regions (title, paragraph, table, figure, header/footer) and their order.
2. Output structured text such as Markdown with headings and tables, or JSON with region types and boxes.
3. Drop or tag running headers and footers.
4. For vision LLMs, ask for a region-by-region transcription in reading order, and check with a human-readable overlay.

**Why it matters.** Wrong order produces fluent but incorrect answers, such as attaching a footnote's condition to the wrong clause. In RAG, bad order also creates bad chunks.

**Failure mode:** evaluating only character accuracy and missing order errors.

tables-forms-merged-cells.explain:
## What it is

Tables and forms are where document reading most often breaks.

**Tables.** Meaning lives in the intersection of row and column headers. Merged cells (a header spanning several columns), multi-line cells, nested headers, borderless layouts and tables continuing across pages all make it ambiguous which header a value belongs to. Flattened text loses these relationships.

**Forms.** Fields are label-value pairs by proximity (label above or left of the box), with checkboxes, radio groups, handwriting and pre-printed text mixed together. A tick mark's meaning depends on which label it sits next to.

**Approaches**
- Extract tables to structured form (JSON rows with header paths, or Markdown/HTML), not prose.
- Expand merged cells explicitly (repeat the header for each spanned column).
- Handle page-spanning tables by carrying headers forward.
- For forms, extract key-value pairs with the label text and box location; treat checkbox state as its own field.
- Validate: row sums, column totals, required fields, enumerated values.

**Failure mode:** a value silently shifted one column left, which still looks plausible. Totals checks catch many of these.

how-models-read-charts.explain:
## What it is

Vision-language models read charts by recognizing the **chart type, labels, legend, and approximate marks**, not by measuring pixels.

**What works.** Identifying chart type, titles, axis labels, trends ("rising then flat"), rough comparisons, the highest/lowest category, and values that are explicitly printed as data labels.

**What is shaky.** Precise values read off an unlabelled axis (estimates only), many-series line charts with similar colours, small multiples, dual axes, log scales, stacked segments, and overlapping points. Truncated axes can mislead both people and models.

**Best practices**
- If the underlying data exists, use it instead of the picture.
- Ask for values with an explicit uncertainty ("approximate, to nearest gridline") and units.
- Crop and enlarge the plot and legend.
- Ask the model to first transcribe the axes and legend, then answer.
- Cross-check against any numbers in the surrounding text.

**Interview angle:** treat chart reading as estimation; do not feed it into calculations that need exact values without verification.

## What it is

For document extraction, define the **schema first, then write the prompt**.

**Why.** The schema is the contract: fields, types, allowed values, required versus optional, and what 'missing' looks like. Prompts written without it drift into inconsistent field names, mixed formats and invented values.

**What a good schema has**
- Typed fields (string, number, date in ISO format, enum).
- A nullable value plus an explicit reason or `not_found` convention for absent data (never force a guess).
- Units and currency as separate fields.
- Arrays for repeating items such as line items, each with its own fields.
- Optional evidence fields: source page, quote, bounding box, confidence.

**Then the prompt.** Describe the document type, give field definitions and edge-case rules (which date is the invoice date, how to treat negative amounts), and use structured output / JSON-schema mode where available. Add a few examples for ambiguous fields.

**Failure mode:** prompt-first iteration leads to a downstream parser coded against whatever the model happened to emit, breaking when it changes.

routing-low-confidence-to-review.explain:
## What it is

Automation should be **selective**: auto-accept what is reliably right, send the rest to people.

**Signals for low confidence**
- OCR word confidences below a threshold.
- Validation failures (sums mismatch, bad checksum).
- Disagreement between two methods or between repeated runs.
- Model abstention ('unreadable') or missing required fields.
- Document type or layout unseen in the test set.

**Design**
1. Define thresholds from labelled data: choose the confidence cut-off that meets a target error rate on auto-accepted items.
2. Route by field importance: a wrong description matters less than a wrong amount.
3. Give reviewers the page image, highlighted regions and the model's value, so correction takes seconds.
4. Feed corrections back as new test cases and prompt examples.
5. Randomly sample auto-accepted items to estimate the hidden error rate.

**Trade-off.** Lower thresholds save human time but let more errors through; the right point depends on error cost.

**Failure mode:** relying on the model's stated confidence without calibration, or never auditing the auto-accepted stream.

## What it is

In **visual RAG**, the unit you index changes from a text chunk to a **page or region** treated as an image (or image plus text).

**Options**
- **Whole page**: simple, preserves layout, works with page-image embedding models; but a page may contain several unrelated things and costs many tokens when sent to the generator.
- **Region/element**: tables, figures, paragraphs detected by layout analysis; more precise retrieval and cheaper generation, but needs reliable layout detection and loses surrounding context.
- **Parent-child**: retrieve small regions, expand to the full page for answering.

**Indexing choices.** Embed the page image with a multimodal embedding or late-interaction visual retriever, or embed the OCR/caption text, or both. Store metadata: document, page, region box, title, section.

**Why it matters.** Text chunking destroys tables and figures; page and region units keep them intact so questions like 'what does the second chart show' are answerable.

**Failure mode:** regions too small to contain the answer's context, or pages too big so the signal is diluted.

## What it is

Retrieval is strongest when it combines **text signals and visual signals**.

**Text retrieval** (BM25, text embeddings over OCR or the text layer) excels at exact terms, names, codes and quoted phrases. **Visual retrieval** (page-image embeddings, late-interaction models) captures layout, charts, diagrams and table-heavy pages that text extraction mangles.

1. Run both retrievers over the same corpus.
2. Fuse results (reciprocal rank fusion or weighted scores).
3. Optionally rerank with a cross-encoder or a vision-capable reranker.

## What it is

Every answer from documents should **cite the page (and region) it was derived from**.

**Why**
- Users can verify quickly, which is the main trust mechanism.
- Citations expose retrieval errors (answer from the wrong page).
- Enables automated grounding checks and audits.

Visual pipelines are powerful but often unnecessary. **Plain text wins** when:

the-token-cost-of-page-images.explain:
## What it is

A page image can cost around a thousand tokens or more depending on resolution and the provider's scheme (check current docs). The text on that same page may be only several hundred tokens.

**Cost model (illustrative).** If a page image is about 1,500 tokens at a given price per million input tokens, 100,000 pages is 150M tokens. Plain text at about 600 tokens per page would be 60M. Multiply by multiple calls (retries, re-ranking, multi-page questions) and the difference compounds.

**Levers**
- Render at the minimum legible resolution; crop margins.
- Send only retrieved pages (top-k), not whole documents.
- Use text for pages where it suffices, images where layout matters.
- Cache repeated page images and reuse extraction results rather than reprocessing.
- Use batch pricing for offline jobs where available.
- Choose smaller or cheaper models for easy pages and route hard ones up.

**Also consider latency**: more tokens means slower time to first token.

**Failure mode:** estimating cost from text word counts and discovering a multiplied bill after switching to page images.

denoising-not-next-token-prediction.explain:
## What it is

Most image and video generators (diffusion and related flow-matching models) do not predict the next token. They **start from noise and iteratively remove it**.

**Training.** Take a real image, add random noise at a random strength, and train the network to predict the noise (or the clean image/velocity) given the noisy input, the noise level and a conditioning signal such as a text embedding.

**Generation.** Begin with pure random noise, then repeat the denoising step many times (typically tens of steps, fewer for distilled models). Each step nudges the sample toward something that matches the prompt. Often this runs in a compressed **latent space** and a decoder turns the final latent into pixels.

**Contrast with LLMs.** An autoregressive LLM emits tokens left to right and cannot revise earlier ones; diffusion refines the whole image in parallel across steps. Some systems do generate images autoregressively, so the line is not absolute.

**Consequences.** Cost scales with steps and resolution; global composition is shaped early, fine detail late; text rendering and exact counts are hard because nothing explicitly enumerates them.

**Interview probe:** why diffusion cannot be 'streamed' token by token like an LLM.

Image generators denoise, they do not next-token predict. Prompts steer subject and style weakly. Seeds replay. Resolution, steps, and aspect ratio price the run. img2img, inpaint, outpaint, and pose/edge control are different tools. Cost is per accepted image. Video adds time and consistency. Rights and watermarks matter. User pixels are untrusted; faces and documents need retention rules.

The checklist line to keep in your head is: Denoising, not next-token prediction. Understand that a generative image model starts from random noise and repeatedly removes it, rather than predicting the next token the way an LLM does.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, denoising, not next-token prediction is how you avoid a class of incidents this module exists to catch. Generation is cheap per image and expensive per accepted asset. Safety on uploads is the same problem as pasted text.

The concrete requirement is: Understand that a generative image model starts from random noise and repeatedly removes it, rather than predicting the next token the way an LLM does. If you cannot show an artefact for that sentence, you are still in demo mode.

In interviews, denoising vs LLMs, seeds, and why iteration cost dominates — plus PII and safety on user images. A strong answer names this item (Denoising, not next-token prediction) and the next action, not a vendor logo.

## How it works + one small example

Treat “Denoising, not next-token prediction” as a control you can point at, not a slogan. Understand that a generative image model starts from random noise and repeatedly removes it, rather than predicting the next token the way an LLM does.

The **seed** initializes the random noise a generation starts from. Same model, same prompt, same settings and same seed should give the same image; change the seed and you get a different one.

- Reproducing a result you liked.
- Fair comparison: hold the seed fixed while changing one variable (prompt wording, steps, guidance).
- Generating variations by changing the seed with everything else constant.

## What it is

Image generation cost and latency are driven by **resolution, number of steps and model size**.

- **Resolution**: compute grows roughly with pixel count (attention cost can grow faster). Doubling width and height is about 4x the pixels.
- **Steps**: each denoising step is one network pass. Fewer steps are faster but may reduce quality; distilled or turbo models target very few steps.
- **Model size and extras**: larger models, upscalers, refiners and safety checks add time and cost.
- **Batch size**: generating several candidates multiplies cost.

**Illustrative example.** If one step at 1024x1024 takes 0.1 s on some GPU, 30 steps take about 3 s plus decode; at 2048x2048 you might expect several times more per step.

**Practices**
- Generate at the base resolution the model was trained on, then upscale instead of generating huge images directly (large sizes can cause repeated or malformed content).
- Tune steps empirically; returns diminish beyond a point.
- Use drafts at low cost, finalize a chosen candidate at higher quality.
- Hosted APIs usually price per image by size/quality tier; check current docs.

**Failure mode:** cranking steps and size for marginal gains.

## What it is

Three ways to condition generation on an existing image instead of starting from pure noise.

**img2img.** Add noise to an input image partway (controlled by a **strength**/denoise parameter) and denoise toward a new prompt. Low strength keeps structure and changes style; high strength departs more from the original.

**Inpainting.** Provide an image and a mask; only the masked area is regenerated according to the prompt, while the rest is preserved or blended. Used for removing objects, replacing items, fixing hands, changing clothing.

**Outpainting.** Extend the canvas beyond the original borders, generating plausible new content consistent with the edge.

**Practical notes**
- Masks should be slightly larger than the object with soft edges to avoid seams.
- Lighting and perspective mismatches are the typical failures; match prompt details to the surroundings.
- Repeated passes can drift in colour and sharpness.
- Keep the original and masks for traceability.

**Interview angle:** explain strength as how much noise is injected, and why inpainting is preferred over regenerating a whole image when only a part needs to change.

Image generators denoise, they do not next-token predict. Prompts steer subject and style weakly. Seeds replay. Prompts are poor at precision, so tools add **conditioning controls**.

**Structural control** fixes geometry: edge maps, depth maps, pose skeletons, segmentation maps or sketches act as extra inputs (e.g. ControlNet-style adapters) so the output follows the layout while the prompt sets content and style.

## What it is

Video generation adds the **time dimension** to image generation, and with it new problems.

**What is new**
- **Temporal consistency**: objects, faces and lighting must stay coherent across frames; flicker and morphing are common.
- **Motion**: plausible physics, camera movement and action; models often break on complex interactions, hands, and long sequences.
- **Compute**: many frames means far more cost and latency than a single image; clips are typically seconds long and priced per second or by tier (check current docs).
- **Conditioning**: text-to-video, image-to-video (animate a still), video-to-video (restyle), plus audio in some systems.
- **Editing and control**: start/end frames, camera paths, reference subjects.

**How it works at a high level.** Usually diffusion or flow models over spatiotemporal latents (compressed in both space and time), sometimes with a transformer over patches across frames.

**Practices.** Use short clips, image-to-video from a good first frame, stitch scenes in an editor, and review frame by frame for artifacts. Expect lower acceptance rates than images.

**Failure mode:** promising consistent characters across a long video from prompts alone.

provenance-watermarks-rights.explain:
## What it is

Generated media raises questions of **provenance, watermarking and rights**.

**Provenance.** Metadata standards such as C2PA-style content credentials record how an asset was made or edited. They are useful but metadata is easily stripped by re-encoding or screenshots, so absence proves nothing.

**Watermarks.** Visible marks are obvious but cropped easily. Invisible watermarks embedded in pixels or in the generation process can survive some edits but not all, and detection is probabilistic. Treat them as signals, not proof.

**Rights and risk**
- Training data and output copyright status vary by jurisdiction and are evolving; check current terms and law.
- Terms of service of the generator define commercial use and indemnities.
- Avoid generating real people's likeness, trademarks or an artist's distinctive style without permission; consent and defamation risks apply.
- Disclose AI-generated content where required by platform rules or regulation.

**Practices.** Log prompts, model versions and outputs; keep source licences for any reference images or fine-tuning data; add content credentials where possible; have a human review before publication.

**Failure mode:** assuming a missing watermark means the image is real.

waveform-to-spectrogram-to-tokens.explain:
## What it is

Sound is a 1D waveform: air pressure sampled many times per second (for example 16,000 samples per second for speech). That raw signal is too long and too low-level to feed a transformer directly.

**Typical path**
1. **Resample** to a standard rate (often 16 kHz for speech) and mono.
2. **Spectrogram**: slice into short overlapping windows (about 25 ms every 10 ms), compute the frequency content of each (often on a mel scale), giving a 2D time-by-frequency picture.
3. **Encoder**: a neural network (convolution plus transformer layers) turns the spectrogram into a shorter sequence of embeddings, one per roughly 20-40 ms.
4. **Tokens**: either continuous embeddings fed to the model, or discrete **audio tokens** from a neural codec (quantized codes) that a language model can read and also generate.

**Illustrative numbers.** 10 seconds of audio at 16 kHz is 160,000 samples, but after encoding might be a few hundred embeddings.

**Why it matters.** The audio-token rate sets context cost and latency, and codec design limits fidelity (music and noise are harder than clean speech).

**Failure mode:** feeding wrong sample rates or stereo/format mismatches, which silently degrades recognition.

Audio goes waveform → spectrogram or learned tokens. You pay per second, including silence. Transcribe-then-prompt discards tone; audio-native keeps more and costs more. Conversations are latency-sensitive. Accents, code-switch, jargon, and bad mics break recognition. Streaming ASR and batch captions have different budgets.

The checklist line to keep in your head is: Waveform to spectrogram to tokens. Understand the path from a waveform to model input: audio is sampled, converted into a spectrogram or learned audio tokens, and then treated as another token stream.

- Long recordings (hours of meetings) can dominate cost and exceed context; chunk and process in parallel.
- Silence, hold music and dead air cost the same, so trim them with voice activity detection.

transcribe-then-prompt-vs-audio-native.explain:
## What it is

Two architectures for spoken input.

**Transcribe then prompt.** A speech recognition model produces text; an LLM reasons over it; optionally text-to-speech speaks the reply. Modular, cheap, easy to log and debug, and each part can be swapped.

**Audio-native.** One model consumes audio directly (and may produce audio). It can use tone, emphasis, hesitation, and non-speech sounds, can respond with lower latency by skipping stages, and can handle interruptions more naturally.

**Choosing**
- Meeting notes, search, compliance records: transcript pipelines (text is the record).
- Voice assistants, emotional nuance, real-time conversation, accents and code-switching: consider audio-native.
- Regulated settings: you may need the transcript anyway for audit; audio-native can still emit a transcript.

**Trade-offs.** Audio-native: harder to inspect, newer, maybe pricier per minute, vendor lock-in. Pipelines: cumulative latency (ASR + LLM + TTS) and error propagation.

**Interview answer:** pick based on what must survive (words versus delivery), latency needs, auditability and cost; prototype both on your data.

Audio goes waveform → spectrogram or learned tokens. You pay per second, including silence. Transcribe-then-prompt discards tone; audio-native keeps more and costs more. Conversations are latency-sensitive. Accents, code-switch, jargon, and bad mics break recognition. Streaming ASR and batch captions have different budgets.

The checklist line to keep in your head is: Transcribe-then-prompt vs audio-native. Distinguish transcribe-then-prompt pipelines, where a speech-to-text model produces text for an LLM, from audio-native models that consume the sound itself.

## What it is

A transcript is text only. It discards much of what speech carries.

**Discarded signals**
- **Prosody**: pitch, volume, speed, emphasis (sarcasm, urgency, uncertainty).
- **Emotion and speaker state**: anger, stress, hesitation, laughter.
- **Speaker identity** unless diarization labels who spoke; overlaps and interruptions flatten.
- **Timing**: pauses and rhythm (a long pause before 'yes' means something).
- **Non-speech sounds**: alarms, background events, music, noise.
- **Normalization losses**: disfluencies ('um') cleaned, dialect and accent smoothed, numbers and punctuation guessed.

**Why it matters.** Sentiment, compliance (did the agent read the disclosure?), medical consults, and coaching often depend on these cues. An LLM given only text can be confidently wrong about tone.

- Add timestamps and speaker labels.
- Run separate audio classifiers (emotion, events) and attach their output as metadata.
- Keep the audio and link transcript segments to time ranges for review.
- Use audio-native models for tone-dependent tasks.

**Failure mode:** treating the transcript as the ground truth of what was said and meant.

why-audio-is-latency-sensitive.explain:
## What it is

Conversation has a tight timing budget. People expect a response within roughly a second (a few hundred milliseconds feels natural), and long gaps feel broken. Audio applications therefore care about latency far more than a batch text job.

**Where latency adds up in a pipeline**
- Capture and network upload.
- Endpointing (deciding the speaker finished; too short cuts people off, too long adds delay).
- Speech recognition.
- LLM time to first token and generation.
- Text-to-speech start.
- Network back and audio playback buffering.

**Techniques**
- **Streaming** at every stage so work overlaps (partial ASR, token streaming into TTS).
- Smaller or faster models for the voice path; cache and prefetch.
- Audio-native models that collapse stages.
- Handle **barge-in** (user interrupts) by cancelling playback and generation.
- Region placement near users.

**Trade-offs.** Faster endpointing and smaller models lower latency but raise errors and interruptions. Measure end-to-end p50 and p95 from end of user speech to start of audio reply.

**Failure mode:** optimizing LLM speed while a long endpointing delay dominates.

Audio goes waveform → spectrogram or learned tokens. You pay per second, including silence. Transcribe-then-prompt discards tone; audio-native keeps more and costs more. where-speech-recognition-breaks.explain:
## What it is

Speech recognition is strong on clear speech in common languages and degrades in predictable ways.

**Common breakpoints**
- **Noise and reverb**: crowds, cars, speakerphones, far-field microphones.
- **Overlapping speakers** and crosstalk.
- **Accents, dialects, code-switching** between languages mid-sentence.
- **Domain vocabulary**: drug names, product names, acronyms, people's names, which get replaced by common similar-sounding words.
- **Numbers and formats**: phone numbers, IDs, dates and spelled-out letters.
- **Low-resource languages** with less training data.
- **Telephone-quality audio** (8 kHz) and heavy compression.
- **Hallucination on silence or music**: some models output fluent text for non-speech segments, or repeat phrases.

**Mitigations**
- Better capture (close mic, noise suppression), voice activity detection.
- Provide custom vocabulary or prompts with expected terms.
- Diarization for overlaps; language identification.
- Post-correction against known entities (lookup lists), and confidence thresholds with review.
- Evaluate with word error rate on your own audio, sliced by condition, and also on entity-level accuracy.

**Failure mode:** trusting overall WER while critical entities are wrong.

Audio goes waveform → spectrogram or learned tokens. You pay per second, including silence. Transcribe-then-prompt discards tone; audio-native keeps more and costs more. what-whisper-actually-returns.explain:
## What it is

Whisper is an encoder-decoder transformer trained on a large corpus of weakly labelled audio. It does not return "the truth"; it returns the **most likely token sequence** given the audio, decoded like a language model.

- Output is text plus optional **segments** with start/end timestamps (and word timestamps via extra alignment). Timestamps are predicted as special tokens, so they can drift.
- Audio is processed in **30-second windows**; longer files are chunked and stitched, and text context from the previous window conditions the next.
- Some APIs return a per-segment confidence signal (average log-probability, no-speech probability, compression ratio). These help flag likely hallucinations.
- Failure mode: on silence, music or noise it can **hallucinate fluent text** ("Thanks for watching"), or loop and repeat a phrase.

Interview angle: say that transcripts are probabilistic, so downstream code should keep timestamps and confidence, not treat the string as ground truth.

Whisper-class models return a transcript, optional word times, and confidence — not edited prose. Batch vs streaming, accents and code-mix, diarization as a separate step, WER that you read against the downstream task. TTS (Kokoro and peers) is another model: voice, prosody, pronunciation, streaming synthesis, hosted vs local. Most products still want text they can search and eval.

The checklist line to keep in your head is: What Whisper actually returns. Understand what a speech-to-text model such as Whisper produces: a transcript, optional word timestamps, and confidence signals rather than clean edited prose.

batch-vs-streaming-transcription.explain:
## What it is

**Batch** transcription sends a complete file and gets the whole transcript back. It sees full context, so accuracy is best and cost is lowest. **Streaming** sends audio in small frames (for example 20-100 ms) and returns partial results as speech arrives.

- Streaming gives **interim hypotheses** that may change, then a **final** result once the model is confident or an endpoint is detected.
- Whisper itself is not natively streaming; "streaming Whisper" is usually repeated re-decoding of a growing buffer or a chunked sliding window, which costs extra compute and lag.
- Purpose-built streaming recognisers (hosted or local) trade a little accuracy for low latency.
- Rule of thumb: **batch** for meetings, podcasts, subtitles and analytics; **streaming** for live captions, voice agents and dictation.

Trade-off to state: streaming reduces time-to-first-word but gives unstable partials, so UI and downstream logic must tolerate revisions.

accents-code-mixing-noise.explain:
## What it is

Speech models are trained on skewed data, so accuracy varies by **accent, dialect, language mixing and acoustic condition**. Averages hide this: a model with 5% error on clean US English can be far worse on a speaker with a regional accent or a noisy phone line.

- **Code-mixing** (Hinglish, Spanglish) switches language mid-sentence. Language auto-detection often locks onto one language and mangles the other; script choice (Latin vs native script) also matters.
- **Noise and bad mics**: far-field audio, codec compression (8 kHz telephony), reverb and overlapping speech degrade all models.
- Mitigations: pass a **language hint** or prompt with expected vocabulary, denoise cautiously (aggressive denoising can hurt), match sample rate, and pick a model trained on telephony if that is your channel.
- Always **measure on your own users' audio**, sliced by accent and channel.

speaker-diarization.explain:
## What it is

**Diarization** answers "who spoke when". It is separate from transcription: it segments audio into speaker turns and labels them SPEAKER_00, SPEAKER_01, etc., then you merge those labels with the transcript by timestamp.

- Typical pipeline: voice activity detection, speaker embeddings per short window, **clustering** into speakers, then alignment with word timestamps.
- Labels are anonymous and consistent only within one file; naming speakers needs enrolment or external info.
- Weak points: **overlapping speech**, short interjections, similar voices, unknown speaker count, and word timestamps that disagree with turn boundaries (a word is assigned to the wrong speaker).
- Metric: **diarization error rate** (missed speech, false alarm, speaker confusion).

Use cases: meeting minutes, call analysis, interviews. If you have separate channels per speaker (stereo call recordings), use those instead; it is far more reliable.

Whisper-class models return a transcript, optional word times, and confidence — not edited prose. ## What it is

**WER** = (substitutions + deletions + insertions) / words in the reference. A 10% WER means about one in ten words differs from a human reference. It is the standard speech-to-text metric but needs care.

- **Normalise first**: casing, punctuation, numbers ("twenty" vs "20"), contractions and spelling variants can inflate WER without changing meaning. Agree one normaliser and use it for every system.
- WER weights all words equally; missing "not" counts the same as missing "the". For products, also track **entity accuracy** (names, numbers, codes) or task success.
- WER can exceed 100% with many insertions (hallucinations).
- Numbers need a **reference set** from your domain: hours of labelled audio, sliced by accent and noise, not a public benchmark.
- Small test sets give noisy estimates; report sample size.

Whisper-class models return a transcript, optional word times, and confidence — not edited prose. Batch vs streaming, accents and code-mix, diarization as a separate step, WER that you read against the downstream task. TTS (Kokoro and peers) is another model: voice, prosody, pronunciation, streaming synthesis, hosted vs local. Most products still want text they can search and eval.

The checklist line to keep in your head is: Word error rate in practice. Read word error rate as a measure of transcription quality, and reason about which errors actually matter for whatever happens downstream.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, word error rate in practice is how you avoid a class of incidents this module exists to catch. A quiet-room demo is not production. Noise and speakers will move WER more than a new model card.

The concrete requirement is: Read word error rate as a measure of transcription quality, and reason about which errors actually matter for whatever happens downstream. If you cannot show an artefact for that sentence, you are still in demo mode.

what-kokoro-turns-text-into.explain:
## What it is

Kokoro is a small open-weights **text-to-speech** model. Like most neural TTS, it converts text into a **mel spectrogram or acoustic representation**, then a vocoder turns that into a waveform.

- Front end: text is normalised ("$5" becomes "five dollars"), then converted to **phonemes** with a grapheme-to-phoneme step, so the acoustic model sees sounds, not spelling.
- The acoustic model predicts duration, pitch and energy for each phoneme, producing prosody.
- The vocoder synthesises audio at a fixed sample rate (commonly 24 kHz).
- Small models run on CPU or modest GPU, making local synthesis cheap, but voice variety and expressiveness are smaller than large hosted systems.

voice-choice-prosody.explain:
## What it is

A **voice** is a speaker identity (timbre, accent, gender impression); **prosody** is how it speaks: rhythm, pitch, stress, pauses, speed. Both shape trust and comprehension.

- Choose by **use case**: a calm, neutral voice for support; faster and brighter for notifications; slower and clearer for accessibility or elderly users.
- Speaking rate: roughly 140-170 words per minute is comfortable for conversation; lower for dense information such as numbers.
- Controls vary by system: speed, pitch, style or emotion tags, SSML pauses. Many small models expose only voice and speed.
- Test with **real content** (long sentences, lists, numbers), not a demo line. Consistency across a session matters; do not swap voices mid-conversation.
- Cloning someone's voice needs consent and raises misuse risk; label synthetic audio in product contexts.

pronunciation-control.explain:
## What it is

Out of the box, TTS mishandles **names, brands, acronyms, medical or code terms**, and heteronyms ("read", "lead"). You need ways to override.

- **Pre-processing**: expand text yourself ("API" to "A P I", "SQL" to "sequel", "3/4" to "three quarters") before sending.
- **Lexicon / phoneme overrides**: supply IPA or a vendor phoneme for a word; many systems support a custom dictionary.
- **SSML** (hosted engines): `<phoneme>`, `<say-as>` for dates and digits, `<break>` for pauses. Local small models may not support SSML, so rely on text rewriting and phoneme input.
- Keep a **regression list** of tricky words and re-listen after model or version changes.
- LLM-generated text should be instructed to write speakable output (no markdown, no emoji).

Whisper-class models return a transcript, optional word times, and confidence — not edited prose. streaming-synthesis.explain:
## What it is

**Streaming TTS** begins returning audio before the whole utterance is synthesised, cutting **time to first audio** from seconds to a few hundred ms.

- Split the incoming text at **sentence or clause boundaries** and synthesise chunk by chunk; start playback of chunk 1 while chunk 2 is generating.
- Pipe LLM output into TTS as tokens arrive: buffer until a sentence ends, then flush. This overlaps generation, synthesis and playback.
- Trade-offs: very short chunks lose context and sound choppy (bad intonation); long chunks add delay. Typical compromise: a clause or sentence, with a short first chunk for speed.
- Handle **cancellation**: if the user interrupts, stop generation and flush the audio buffer immediately.
- Watch for gaps (underrun) if synthesis is slower than real time.

## What it is

Speech models can be consumed as a **hosted API** or **run locally**. The choice mirrors the general API vs self-host trade-off.

## What it is

In a voice agent, **latency is the product**. Human turn-taking gaps are roughly 200-300 ms; once the delay between the user finishing and the agent speaking passes about **one second**, conversations feel broken, and past two seconds users repeat themselves or hang up.

- Define the metric: **mouth-to-ear / end-of-speech to first audio** (often called voice-to-voice latency), measured at p50 *and* p95. Averages hide the bad calls.
- Every design choice (model size, streaming, region, endpointing) is a trade between latency, quality and cost.
- Set a **latency budget** per stage and enforce it in monitoring, like an SLO.
- A slightly worse answer delivered fast usually beats a perfect answer delivered late, but not when accuracy is safety-critical.

Interview angle: start from the budget (for example under 1 s p50, under 2 s p95) and work backwards to architecture.

Voice agents are latency machines. Budget capture, network, ASR, thinking, TTS, playback. Cascaded STT→LLM→TTS vs speech-to-speech. Overlap synthesis. VAD and endpointing, barge-in, partials, state after a cut turn. Dead air, noise, tool-call holding phrases, reconstruct the call from audio+transcript+timings. TTS is another SLO. Users talk over the bot; you must cancel.

cascaded-vs-speech-to-speech.explain:
## What it is

Two architectures:

- **Cascaded**: audio -> ASR -> text -> LLM -> text -> TTS -> audio. Each stage is swappable, inspectable, and you can log text, apply guardrails and tools between stages.
- **Speech-to-speech (S2S)**: one model takes audio in and emits audio out (natively multimodal/realtime models). It can hear tone, hesitations and emotion, and responds with lower latency since there are fewer hops.

Cascaded wins on control, observability, cost tuning and per-stage best-of-breed. S2S wins on latency, naturalness, and handling interruptions and paralinguistic cues. S2S often has fewer voice options, harder debugging (no intermediate text unless provided), and vendor lock-in.

Many production systems begin cascaded, then adopt S2S where naturalness matters, or keep the cascade for regulated flows needing audit text.

## What it is

Latency falls when stages run **concurrently** instead of strictly in sequence.

- **Streaming ASR** transcribes while the user speaks, so the final text is ready almost at endpoint.
- **Speculative LLM start**: begin generating on a stable partial transcript, and discard if the final differs.
- **Stream LLM to TTS**: send each sentence to TTS as soon as it completes.
- **Stream TTS to audio out**: play the first chunk while the rest synthesises.
- **Warm connections**: keep websocket/HTTP connections and models loaded; precompute prompt caches.
- **Parallel work**: retrieval, tool calls and filler audio can run during generation.

## What it is

**VAD** detects whether a frame contains speech. **Endpointing** decides the user has *finished their turn* and the agent should respond.

- VAD models (energy-based, or small neural ones like Silero) output a speech probability per 10-30 ms frame.
- Simple endpointing: end the turn after N ms of silence (often 500-800 ms). Short N cuts the user off; long N adds dead air.
- Better: **semantic / turn-detection** models that look at the transcript or prosody (a falling tone, a complete sentence) to adapt the timeout.
- Add **pre-roll** audio so the first syllable is not clipped, and a minimum speech duration to ignore clicks and coughs.
- Tune thresholds per channel (phone vs headset).

why-endpointing-is-hard.explain:
## What it is

People pause mid-sentence to think, to recall a number, to breathe. They also end turns with no falling tone, or trail off. Silence alone cannot tell "finished" from "thinking".

- **Context matters**: after 'my number is 555...', a pause means more digits are coming; after 'yes', a pause means done.
- **Speaker differences**: slow speakers, second-language speakers and elderly users pause longer.
- **Noise** makes silence detection unreliable; background speech keeps VAD active forever (never endpoints) or flickers.
- The trade-off is unavoidable: lower timeout = more interruptions of the user; higher = more dead air. Balance by cost of each error in your domain.
- Mitigation: adaptive timeouts, semantic completeness checks, allow the user to continue after the agent starts (barge-in) so early cut-ins are recoverable.

Voice agents are latency machines. Budget capture, network, ASR, thinking, TTS, playback. Cascaded STT→LLM→TTS vs speech-to-speech. Overlap synthesis. VAD and endpointing, barge-in, partials, state after a cut turn. Dead air, noise, tool-call holding phrases, reconstruct the call from audio+transcript+timings. TTS is another SLO. Users talk over the bot; you must cancel.

## What it is

**Barge-in** lets the user interrupt while the agent is speaking. It is essential in natural conversation.

- Detect speech from the user while TTS plays (VAD on the mic stream).

## What it is

Partial (interim) transcripts arrive while the user is still talking. They are useful but **unstable**: words get revised, and the end of the sentence may flip meaning ("transfer fifty" -> "transfer fifteen hundred").

- Retrieval prefetch (look up likely documents).

- Executing **side-effecting actions** (payments, deletes, bookings) from partials.

## What it is

When the user interrupts, the LLM may have *generated* a long answer but the user *heard* only the first part. If you store the full generated text in history, the model believes the user heard things they did not.

- Track **playback position**: map audio played back to text (word timestamps or chunk boundaries).
- **Truncate the assistant message** in history to what was spoken, optionally marking it as interrupted.
- Tool calls or state changes that were announced but not heard (e.g. "I've cancelled your order, and...") must still be reflected truthfully.
- Realtime APIs often provide events to truncate the item at a given audio offset; use them.
- Failure: the agent says "as I mentioned" about content the user never heard, or fails to repeat important information.

## What it is

Real calls go quiet or die: the user walks away, the line drops, the network stalls.

- **No-input timeout**: after N seconds of user silence, re-prompt ("Are you still there?"); after repeated timeouts, end politely.

- **Connection loss**: detect via heartbeats and transport events; attempt reconnect, keep session state server-side so the call can resume, and offer a callback if it cannot.
- Log termination reasons (hangup, timeout, error) for analysis.
- Watch for **ghost sessions**: connections left open burning ASR/LLM minutes. Always set maximum call length and idle timeouts.

## What it is

Voice agents run in cars, kitchens, call centres and on cheap headsets. Audio quality problems:

- **Background noise** raises WER and triggers false VAD.
- **Crosstalk**: other people talking nearby are transcribed as the user. Mitigate with near-field mics, beamforming, speaker verification, or only accepting the loudest/primary speaker.
- **Bad mics / clipping / low gain**: clipped or quiet audio, wrong sample rate, aggressive codecs.
- **Speakerphone echo**: needs AEC.
- Mitigations: noise suppression (test it, since it can distort speech and *hurt* ASR), gain control, push-to-talk in extreme cases, and asking the user to repeat or confirm key data.
- Detect poor audio (low SNR) and adapt: slower pace, more confirmations, or hand off.

VAD and endpointing, barge-in, partials, state after a cut turn. Dead air, noise, tool-call holding phrases, reconstruct the call from audio+transcript+timings. TTS is another SLO. ## What it is

A **shared embedding space** maps items of different modalities (text, images, audio) into the same vector space so that **semantically related items are close**, regardless of type. A photo of a dog and the sentence "a dog on a beach" land near each other.

- Each modality has its own encoder; training pushes matched pairs together and mismatched pairs apart.
- Once aligned, comparison is plain cosine similarity or dot product, which works with ordinary vector indexes.
- Benefit: one index and one query path for mixed content; query by text, retrieve images.
- Limits: the space reflects training pairs. Fine details, text inside images, counts, or domain-specific concepts may be weak. Embeddings from different models are **not comparable**; never mix spaces.

A shared embedding space puts a matching image and caption nearby. CLIP-style training pulls pairs together. You can query images with text and text with images using the same vector search you used in Level 4. Caption-then-search is the alternative. Fine detail, text-in-image, counts, and your domain will fail general encoders. Evaluate on your collection. Do not mix metrics across incompatible indexes.

The checklist line to keep in your head is: A shared embedding space. Understand a shared embedding space, where an image and a caption that describe the same thing land close together as vectors.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, a shared embedding space is how you avoid a class of incidents this module exists to catch. A CLIP demo on dogs will not retrieve your machine parts.

## How it works + one small example

1. **Cross-modal embeddings**: embed images directly and match with text queries.

## What it is

Known failure modes:

- **Modality gap**: text and image vectors cluster apart in the space, so raw similarity scores are not comparable across modalities; scores from text-text vs text-image are different scales.
- **Compositionality**: "a cat on a dog" vs "a dog on a cat" can look the same; counts and spatial relations are weak.
- **Negation and exclusion**.
- **Text in images / fine detail / charts**: small or dense content is lost at low resolution.
- **Domain shift**: medical, industrial, or brand-specific imagery that was rare in training.
- **Language coverage**: non-English queries may be weaker.
- **Hubness / near-duplicates**: some items appear in many results.

A shared embedding space puts a matching image and caption nearby. CLIP-style training pulls pairs together. privacy-for-voice-faces-scans.explain:
## What it is

Voice, faces and medical scans are **sensitive or biometric data** in many jurisdictions.

- Know what data you send: voice prints identify people; faces and scans are personal data, possibly special-category (health).
- Check vendor terms: retention, training on your data, sub-processors, data residency, and zero-retention options.
- Minimise: crop faces, redact PII before sending, process locally when feasible, store derived text instead of raw media.
- Get consent, set retention limits, encrypt in transit and at rest, and log access.
- Regulations (GDPR, HIPAA, biometric laws) may require agreements and impact assessments; involve legal.
- Local or on-device processing is often the cleanest answer for the most sensitive inputs.

why-long-runs-are-different.explain:
## What it is

A deep-research or long-horizon agent runs for dozens to hundreds of steps over minutes or hours. Different from a single prompt:

- **Errors compound**: a 95%-reliable step repeated 20 times succeeds only about 36% of the time (illustrative arithmetic).
- **Context fills up**: tool outputs, pages and notes exceed the window; you must summarise and offload to external memory.
- **Drift**: the agent loses the original goal or chases tangents.
- **Cost and time** grow; you need budgets, checkpoints and resumability.
- **Non-determinism**: reruns differ; you need traces to debug.
- **Verification is harder**: nobody reads every step, so outputs need evidence.

Designs therefore include planning, state files, step limits, checkpoints, and evaluation of the final artifact and process.

Long-horizon research is not one prompt. Decompose, breadth then depth, read critically, reconcile disagreement, attach claims to sources, take notes because context dies, know when to stop, write an auditable report. Failures: drift, thin synthesis, fake cites. Pixels and seconds dwarf text; cache and downscale. Cascade: cheap classifier, expensive multimodal only when needed.

The checklist line to keep in your head is: Why long runs are different. Understand what changes when a task runs for many minutes across many sources instead of resolving inside a single prompt and a single response.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, why long runs are different is how you avoid a class of incidents this module exists to catch. A 20-minute agent that “researches” will burn image tokens and invent citations unless you design the loop.

The concrete requirement is: Understand what changes when a task runs for many minutes across many sources instead of resolving inside a single prompt and a single response. If you cannot show an artefact for that sentence, you are still in demo mode.

In interviews, how the run differs from a chat, how you stop, and how you keep claims attached — plus the cost of media. A strong answer names this item (Why long runs are different) and the next action, not a vendor logo.

## What it is

Every factual claim in the output should be **traceable to a source**. This is the main defence against hallucination in research reports.

- Structure intermediate notes as claim + source URL + quote/span + date + confidence.
- At writing time, cite inline per claim, not a bibliography dump at the end.
- Verify citations: the URL exists, the passage supports the claim (a separate checker pass or entailment check).
- Mark claims that are the agent's **inference** rather than sourced fact.
- Failure modes: fabricated URLs, citing a page that doesn't say it, outdated quotes.
- Keep source text snapshots or hashes so claims remain auditable after pages change.

Failures: drift, thin synthesis, fake cites. Pixels and seconds dwarf text; cache and downscale. Cascade: cheap classifier, expensive multimodal only when needed.

## What it is

Different modalities fit different devices and contexts.

- **Phone**: camera and microphone are first-class, hands-free voice, scanning documents, photo Q&A; but battery, thermal limits, intermittent network.
- **Laptop/desktop**: keyboard, screen sharing, long documents, more RAM and sometimes a GPU.
- **Wearables/cars/IoT**: voice-first, small screens, noisy settings, limited compute.
- **Browser**: WebGPU/WASM can run small models locally.
- Choose modalities where they reduce user effort: voice while driving, camera for receipts, text for precise edits.
- Match the model to the device: small, quantised models for on-device; larger for server.
- Design graceful fallback when sensors or network are unavailable.

The capstone is a multimodal build with a contract: input types, failures, cost, and eval per modality. Speech and vision often suit on-device: small models, private input, network is the slow part. Quantisation trades precision for size. Phones thermal-throttle. On-device buys offline and no per-request fee. Mix on-device, self-host, and API. Drop a modality before you drop grounding.

## What it is

**Quantisation** stores model weights (and sometimes activations) in fewer bits, e.g. 16-bit down to 8 or 4, shrinking memory and speeding inference.

- Methods: post-training quantisation (GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF formats), quantisation-aware training.
- Multimodal models: vision encoders and audio components may be more sensitive; test each part.

- Multimodal adds image/audio encoders that need extra memory and compute.

what-on-device-buys-you.explain:
## What it is

Running models on the device gives:

- **Privacy**: data never leaves; helpful for voice, photos, health.
- **Latency**: no network round trip; works well for real-time features such as camera or speech.
- **Offline operation** and reliability in poor networks.
- **Cost**: no per-call inference fees; scales with users' hardware.
- **Control**: pinned model version, no vendor deprecation.

Costs: smaller/weaker models, large app downloads, device fragmentation, battery use, update logistics, and harder monitoring (less telemetry). Use on-device for narrow, high-frequency or sensitive tasks; escalate hard requests to a server model.

- **Self-hosted server**: control and privacy within your infrastructure; you manage GPUs; good for steady volume.

what-you-would-cut.explain:
## What it is

When scope slips, **drop a modality before you drop grounding**. A second camera or video track that you cannot cite is a liability. Cites and checks stay.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, what you would cut is how you avoid a class of incidents this module exists to catch. Shipping “it also does photos” without an eval or a cost line is how capstones fail reviews.

The concrete requirement is: When scope slips, **drop a modality before you drop grounding**. A second camera or video track that you cannot cite is a liability. Cites and checks stay. If you cannot show an artefact for that sentence, you are still in demo mode.

In interviews, the contract and what you would cut — never grounding. A strong answer names this item (what you would cut) and the next action, not a vendor logo.

## How it works + one small example

Rank modalities by user value and eval coverage. Cut the uncovered one. Example: you drop video from the demo when page cites broke; you keep invoice crops and text RAG.

## Failure modes

1. **Skipping “what you would cut” because the happy path works.** When scope slips, **drop a modality before you drop grounding**. A second camera or video track that you cannot cite is a liability. Cites and checks stay. One eval set in text for a vision feature.

2. **Doing it once and never again.** A control that is not in CI, a runbook, or a dashboard dies after the demo. Quantising until totals misread.

3. **Confusing a tool with the control.** Buying a vendor does not implement what you would cut. Keeping a third modality that you cannot ground.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I cut a modality before I cut grounding.

## A concrete walk-through

You say the cut out loud: “video went; grounding stayed.”

## Interview follow-up

They push back: “Do we really need what you would cut?” They want on-device everything. You show thermal and the quality drop after 4-bit. They want more modalities. You show the cite rate. Your reply is the incident you would otherwise own: When scope slips, **drop a modality before you drop grounding**. A second camera or video track that you cannot cite is a liability. Cites and checks stay. Then you offer the cheapest version of the control that still has an artefact and a metric.

## What I would measure

Per-modality eval, cost by hop, grounding rate, whether a stranger ran the README. Also: time since you last exercised “what you would cut” on purpose (a drill), not only in an incident.
## Worked numbers

Put a denominator and a window on “what you would cut” the next time you practise it. Illustrative targets are fine until you replace them with a measured one.

## Practise until it is boring

Rank modalities by user value and by whether you can eval them. Cut the uncovered one in public, not quietly. Video is the usual fashion add-on and the first thing that breaks cites. Say the cut out loud in the review: grounding stayed.

## Practise until it is boring

Rehearse what you would cut until you can name the artefact, the metric, and the undo without notes. If you cannot drill it, assume the control is dead. Write the last date you exercised it next to the cheat-sheet line.
